newsitem.title: UK: LME copper burns path higher as tightness hits.
newsitem.headline: LME copper burns path higher as tightness hits.

text.p: Copper roared higher on Tuesday afternoon, slicing through successive resistance levels above $2,300 as nearby tightness lit a fire under the market and speculators piled in.
Aluminium also put in a strong performance as inventories slid while the rest of the complex was buoyed by the market's burst of energy.
Three months copper streaked to a high of $2,349 per tonne, a $60.50 gain from Monday, before finishing the afternoon kerb just $1 off its peak.
"It was spectacular. I think a lot of people were caught by surprise," a trader said.
Stops were hit on the way up around $2,330, prompting a wave of speculative buying, analysts said.

Tight dates from late April until mid-May sent the spreads ballooning, with cash/May flaring to about a $45 backwardation from around $19 on Monday evening. It was in a modest contango most of last week.
The nearby tightness sent the premium of cash over three months metal surging to $100/$105 by the kerb close from $60/$65 on Monday.
The origin of the tightness that suddenly emerged last Friday was unclear.

Some traders believed a big U.S. investment bank was orchestrating shortages while others placed more emphasis on the other side of the equation, saying nervous covering by prominent shorts was behind it.
The tightness comes against a background of production hiccups, including a strike at Chile's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, which was working at 85 percent of normal levels.

Also underpinning prices was a six-week maintenance shutdown at a Kennecott smelter in Utah and labour talks at Phelps Dodges Chino mine, where workers have been without a contract since June 30 last year.
Tuesday's gains have spiced up the chart picture.

"Within a huge trading range structure that began at the 1989 high, the market is expected to reach $2,852 over the next six to 12 months," broker Waterside Futures said in a report released on Tuesday morning.
Only a breech of $2,240 would put this scenario on hold as a deeper pull-back would be seen before prices resumed its uptrend, said the firm's Wavetrack publication, which uses Elliott Wave analysis.
Aluminium had its own bullish reasons to push higher after LME stocks fell by 4,700 tonnes on Tuesday, bringing the total fall to 15.5 percent since January's peak.
When International Primary Aluminium Institute stocks of 3.077 million tonnes are taken into consideration, overall inventories equate to around 6-1/2 weeks of global consumption.
Prices surged to a peak of $1,596 per tonne, up $41, ending the day just $3 off the high.
The market appeared to have come into contact with the 100-day moving average at $1,597, which it would need to breech, analysts said.
After that and the $1,600 psychological area, prices were on target to head towards $1,620, analyst Helen Williamson of broker Brandeis said.
The other metals were less spectacular, following copper and aluminium higher but showing little individual initiative.
Nickel regained the $7,400 mark and finished $45 higher at $7,425, but failed to break out of the recent range capped at $7,450.
Traders were keeping an eye on the situation in New Caledonia where Eramet's ferro-nickel and matte exports were being held up by trade union action.
Zinc added $16 to $1,264, but, like nickel, did not have enough steam to break through the upper reaches of its range at $1,266/8.
Lead gained $14 to $642, near the top of its band.
Tin, however, edged above a recent high of $5,820, ending the day at its high of $5,840, a gain of $130.
Alloy was last indicated firmer at $1,470/75 versus $1,447/50.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
